title: HelioSupport x Redwood — POC check-in (streaming timeouts + 429s)
summary: Weekly POC check-in focused on two production-like issues observed during HelioSupport traffic replay: (1) intermittent streaming disconnect/timeouts around the 60–90s mark for longer responses, and (2) elevated 429s during shift-change bursts due to concurrent request spikes. Redwood walked through how rate limits are enforced (RPM/TPM and concurrent streams), recommended client-side backoff + jitter and right-sizing max concurrency, and proposed Redwood-side configuration tweaks (raise burst/concurrency limits for the POC, adjust queue/timeout settings, and validate keepalive behavior). Team also aligned on what can be shared publicly if HelioSupport participates in the reference program: ok to share qualitative outcomes and ranges/relative improvements, but avoid exact ticket volumes, agent headcount, and any incident-specific details; approval will route through Legal + Security.
topics: POC traffic replay results recap (last 7 days)
429 rate limiting: concurrency spikes, token-per-minute, retry strategy
Streaming timeouts/disconnects: client timeouts, proxy/load balancer, keepalive
Observability: correlation IDs, request logs, Console dashboards
Reference program alignment: what can/can’t be shared publicly
action_items: Redwood (Simran): Pull 429 samples by request_id/correlation_id from 2025-06-02 16:00–18:00 PT and confirm which limiter triggered (concurrency vs TPM). Due: 2025-06-04
HelioSupport (Anika): Share client retry settings + current timeout values (connect/read) and whether requests traverse Cloudflare / internal proxy. Due: 2025-06-04
Redwood (Hannah): Coordinate temporary POC rate-limit increase (burst + concurrent streams) for HelioSupport workspace and document the new limits in email. Due: 2025-06-04
HelioSupport (Morgan): Provide 3 representative prompts that produce the longest streaming responses causing disconnects (with redacted PII). Due: 2025-06-05
Redwood (Simran): Recommend a reference implementation for exponential backoff with jitter + idempotency key handling for chat streaming retries. Due: 2025-06-05
Both: Draft a “public share” boundary list (metrics ok as ranges/percent; no exact volumes) and route to HelioSupport Legal for initial read. Due: 2025-06-10
next_steps: Redwood to analyze limiter source for recent 429s and propose target concurrency limits per pod/worker.
HelioSupport to send timeout/proxy details and sample long-running prompts.
Redwood to apply a temporary POC limit increase and re-run shift-change burst test.
Confirm whether HelioSupport prefers reference-call-only vs public case study; if public, start with anonymized draft + later decide on logo/quotes.
transcript:
Fireflies.ai Transcript

Meeting: HelioSupport x Redwood — POC check-in (streaming timeouts + 429s)
Date: Jun 3, 2025 10:00 AM PT
Duration: 34 min
Attendees:
- Hannah Schmitt (Redwood, AE)
- Simran Kaur (Redwood, Solutions Architect)
- Derek Lin (HelioSupport, Head of Support Ops)
- Anika Patel (HelioSupport, Staff Engineer)
- Morgan Reyes (HelioSupport, Eng Manager, Platform)

---

[00:00] Hannah Schmitt: Hey Derek, Anika, Morgan—good to see you. Simran’s on as well. Um, goal today is mostly the two issues you flagged in Slack and the support ticket: the streaming timeouts and the 429 spikes. Then we should spend like five minutes on the reference program thing—what you’d be comfortable sharing publicly.

[00:22] Derek Lin: Sounds good.

[00:23] Anika Patel: Yep.

[00:25] Simran Kaur: Hey everyone.

[00:30] Hannah Schmitt: Cool. Anika, do you want to start with what you’re seeing on your side? Like when it happens and how often.

[00:38] Anika Patel: Sure. So we replayed… basically our “shift change” pattern—like 4pm to 6pm Pacific is worst. We see a bunch of 429s. Not like constant, but a burst, and then the client retries and eventually it works. But it makes the app feel laggy.

[00:56] Anika Patel: And then on the streaming thing: longer answers, like when the agent asks for a full summary plus next steps, sometimes the stream just… stops. No final “done” event. Our UI waits, then times out.

[01:10] Morgan Reyes: To add: we’re seeing it around one minute-ish, but not always. It’s intermittent, so it’s hard to know if it’s your side, or our side, or like Cloudflare.

[01:20] Hannah Schmitt: Got it. Thanks. Simran, want to pull up what you saw in Console?

[01:25] Simran Kaur: Yep. I looked at the workspace logs you shared—thank you for enabling request logging. For the 429s, there’s a cluster around 2025-06-02 16:40 to 17:20. The responses are definitely rate-limit responses.

[01:41] Simran Kaur: Redwood has a few different limiters depending on plan and config: requests per minute, tokens per minute, and also concurrent streams. From the raw error bodies I saw, it just says “rate limit exceeded” which is annoying because it’s not explicit.

[01:56] Anika Patel: Yeah that’s what we saw. There’s no… like “you hit concurrency” message.

[02:01] Simran Kaur: Right. We can dig in server-side by request_id and determine which limiter tripped. If you can send me a handful of request_ids from the timeframe, I can confirm.

[02:11] Anika Patel: We can. We log a correlation ID, and I think it maps. I’ll share what we have.

[02:16] Hannah Schmitt: Great. For the POC we can also raise the burst. We kept it conservative initially.

[02:22] Derek Lin: Quick question: is it concurrency per API key, or per… like account? Because we have multiple services hitting it.

[02:30] Simran Kaur: Good question. It’s per workspace / key scope—so effectively per account, unless you’re using separate keys with separate quotas. But concurrency is shared if they’re under the same workspace limits.

[02:44] Morgan Reyes: That matches what we’d expect.

[02:46] Hannah Schmitt: When you do shift change, how many concurrent chats do you open? Like what’s the shape.

[02:53] Derek Lin: Uh, it depends. But like, we might have… I don’t want to give exact numbers. But it spikes, let’s say, 3 to 5x within 10 minutes. People are loading tickets and hitting “summarize” or “draft reply” all at once.

[03:10] Hannah Schmitt: Totally fine, we can keep it ranges.

[03:13] Simran Kaur: On 429 handling: I did notice your client is retrying very aggressively—like immediate retry. That can create a thundering herd.

[03:23] Anika Patel: Yeah. That’s fair. We used a default wrapper and it does like… retry 3 times quickly.

[03:30] Simran Kaur: What we recommend is exponential backoff with jitter. Also respecting Retry-After if provided. I’m not sure if we’re sending Retry-After in all cases right now, but we can.

[03:43] Morgan Reyes: Our other provider—OpenAI—returns some headers we key off. But we’re not consistent across providers.

[03:50] Simran Kaur: Yep. Similar idea. Also, if it’s concurrency-limited, you’ll want a client-side semaphore: cap active streams at N, queue locally.

[04:02] Anika Patel: That makes sense. We don’t have a hard cap right now. It’s basically “fire everything”.

[04:09] Hannah Schmitt: And to be clear, for the POC we can raise the cap so you’re not blocked while you implement that.

[04:16] Derek Lin: Yeah, raising it would help because we want to test “worst case”.

[04:20] Simran Kaur: Just keep in mind: raising concurrency without any client cap can still produce timeouts if the downstream is saturated. But yes, we can give you more headroom.

[04:33] Hannah Schmitt: On the streaming disconnects—Anika, what client are you using? Like node, python, fetch, our SDK?

[04:40] Anika Patel: Node. We’re using your JS SDK for chat completions streaming. It runs behind Cloudflare, then our API gateway, then the browser.

[04:50] Simran Kaur: Okay. That’s helpful. A lot of times the “stream stops at ~60 seconds” is actually a proxy idle timeout. Like the proxy expects bytes within X seconds. But you are getting bytes during the stream, right?

[05:04] Anika Patel: We are, but sometimes the model pauses. Like, there’s a gap of… I don’t know, 10 seconds, then it continues. And maybe that triggers it.

[05:13] Morgan Reyes: Or the browser thinks it’s done. Hard to tell.

[05:16] Simran Kaur: Do you know your Cloudflare and gateway timeout settings? Specifically “read timeout” or “idle timeout”.

[05:23] Anika Patel: Not off the top of my head. I can check. I think Cloudflare has like a 100-second limit on something.

[05:31] Simran Kaur: There are a couple different ones. Also if you’re terminating HTTP/2 and converting to HTTP/1.1 at the gateway, streaming can get weird.

[05:40] Hannah Schmitt: We’ve seen that, yeah.

[05:43] Derek Lin: So you’re saying it might not be Redwood timing out.

[05:47] Simran Kaur: Could be either. On our side, we have request timeouts and max stream duration safeguards, but those are typically longer than 60 seconds, especially for chat. I want to look at specific request logs.

[06:01] Simran Kaur: If you can provide 2–3 prompts that reliably produce the long outputs, we can reproduce. Also, if you can share what the client sees when it fails—does it throw an error, or just ends.

[06:12] Anika Patel: It’s mostly “socket hang up” or “stream closed” depending on where. Sometimes it’s just the UI spinner.

[06:20] Morgan Reyes: We do have Sentry events for it. We can export a couple.

[06:24] Hannah Schmitt: Great.

[06:26] Simran Kaur: Another thing: are you sending keepalive pings from the server to the browser? Like comment frames?

[06:33] Anika Patel: Not currently. We just forward the stream as-is.

[06:37] Simran Kaur: Okay. We can suggest a pattern where if there’s no token chunk for, say, 5 seconds, you send a whitespace or SSE comment to keep the pipe alive. But that’s an application layer thing.

[06:52] Morgan Reyes: Right.

[06:54] Hannah Schmitt: On 429s, I want to make sure we align: are you okay if we temporarily bump your limits during the POC? Then you can retest the burst scenario and we see if it’s solved.

[07:04] Derek Lin: Yes, please.

[07:06] Anika Patel: Yep.

[07:08] Simran Kaur: Cool. Hannah, we’ll need the workspace ID—actually I have it—but we’ll coordinate with ops.

[07:14] Hannah Schmitt: I’ll take that.

[07:15] Morgan Reyes: Question: if we hit 429, can we tell whether it was tokens per minute versus concurrent streams? Because we might have some giant prompts.

[07:25] Simran Kaur: Today, not reliably from the response body. But internally yes. We can also add a header like x-redwood-limit-type in the POC environment. I can check if that’s possible without code changes.

[07:40] Anika Patel: That would be great.

[07:42] Hannah Schmitt: Nice. Simran, is that a big lift?

[07:45] Simran Kaur: I think it’s a config + small gateway change. Not promising today, but we can try.

[07:52] Derek Lin: If not, we can still do backoff and cap concurrency.

[07:56] Simran Kaur: Exactly.

[07:58] Hannah Schmitt: Okay, let’s get a little more specific on your current traffic replay. Morgan, are you using like a queue system or just direct requests.

[08:07] Morgan Reyes: We have a worker queue for offline stuff, but the agent-assist is synchronous in the UI. So it’s the UI calling our API, then we call you.

[08:17] Hannah Schmitt: Got it. So at shift change it’s basically many users clicking at the same time.

[08:22] Morgan Reyes: Exactly.

[08:23] Simran Kaur: If you can batch any of the background tasks, that helps. For synchronous UI, the main lever is concurrency cap and queue.

[08:31] Anika Patel: Yeah. We can implement a per-tenant cap. We just didn’t think we needed it.

[08:38] Simran Kaur: Totally.

[08:40] Hannah Schmitt: On the streaming timeouts, do you have any sense whether it correlates with 429s? Like the system is busy and then streams drop.

[08:49] Anika Patel: It might. We saw them both around the same time. But it also happened at like 11am when there weren’t many users.

[08:58] Simran Kaur: That suggests proxy/timeouts more than load. But we’ll confirm.

[09:05] Hannah Schmitt: Okay. Let’s pivot for a couple minutes to the “public share” question. Derek, you mentioned you might be open to being a reference, but you’re cautious.

[09:14] Derek Lin: Yeah. We’re open to helping, but we can’t share like ticket volume, agent count, any customer names, and we can’t share internal incidents. If it’s “we improved response time” and “reduced cost” in a generic way, fine.

[09:31] Hannah Schmitt: That aligns with our program. There’s a spectrum: reference call only, anonymized public case study, or full logo/quote. We don’t need to decide today.

[09:41] Morgan Reyes: For us, a full logo case study is harder. An anonymized one might be possible. We’d need Legal.

[09:48] Anika Patel: We can probably share architecture at a high level. Like “agent assist service calls LLM” but not specific vendors in the stack beyond Redwood.

[09:58] Simran Kaur: That’s workable. We can keep it to patterns: streaming chat, fallback, rate limiting, and how you handle PII.

[10:07] Derek Lin: Right.

[10:09] Hannah Schmitt: On metrics, what we typically like to publish are percent improvements or ranges. For example “reduced p95 latency by ~30%” or “cut cost per ticket by 20–40% depending on prompt”. Are those okay, assuming we validate?

[10:25] Derek Lin: Percent is safer than absolutes. We don’t want someone to infer our exact scale.

[10:32] Morgan Reyes: Also no specific daily volume numbers.

[10:35] Hannah Schmitt: Understood.

[10:37] Simran Kaur: For reliability, we sometimes mention “reduced timeouts” or “lower error rates”. We should be careful not to imply you had outages.

[10:46] Derek Lin: Exactly.

[10:48] Hannah Schmitt: Okay. We can draft a boundaries doc. Something like: okay to mention streaming, okay to mention fallback, ok to mention “burst traffic at shift changes” but not numbers.

[11:01] Morgan Reyes: That sounds good.

[11:03] Hannah Schmitt: Great. Back to the technical issues. Simran, can you talk through what you need to diagnose the 429s precisely.

[11:10] Simran Kaur: Yeah. Two things: (1) a sample of request_ids or correlation IDs from a 429 response, and (2) a rough idea of the concurrency at the time. Even if it’s a range.

[11:24] Anika Patel: We can do the IDs. Concurrency is harder. But we can approximate based on app logs.

[11:31] Simran Kaur: Perfect.

[11:33] Morgan Reyes: Are your limits based on “requests” or “streams”? Because a streaming request lasts longer.

[11:40] Simran Kaur: Exactly. Concurrency limiter is “active requests/streams” at any moment. So if each stream lasts 30 seconds and you fire 100 at once, concurrency gets huge.

[11:52] Morgan Reyes: Okay.

[11:54] Hannah Schmitt: That matches the behavior: during bursts you create long streams, so concurrency spikes.

[12:01] Derek Lin: We can shorten outputs maybe. Like constrain the summary length.

[12:06] Simran Kaur: Yes—good point. If you set a max tokens output or a shorter template, stream duration goes down.

[12:15] Anika Patel: We currently allow up to 800 tokens on the draft reply.

[12:19] Simran Kaur: That’s not crazy, but depending on model and decoding it can be lengthy. We can help tune.

[12:26] Hannah Schmitt: Also, we can recommend using structured output to reduce verbosity, but maybe that’s later.

[12:33] Morgan Reyes: We’re interested, but one thing at a time.

[12:36] Hannah Schmitt: Totally.

[12:38] Simran Kaur: For streaming timeouts, I want to confirm your client timeouts. Node fetch defaults can be weird. Are you setting a read timeout?

[12:48] Anika Patel: In our server-to-Redwood call, we set 120 seconds. But in browser-to-our server, it might be 60 seconds depending on gateway.

[12:58] Simran Kaur: Aha. That’s likely it. If the browser connection is 60s, you’ll cut off even if Redwood is fine.

[13:05] Morgan Reyes: Our gateway has a 60 second idle timeout. But is it idle or absolute.

[13:12] Anika Patel: It’s “idle”, but if the stream pauses, it might count.

[13:16] Simran Kaur: Exactly. You can keep it alive with SSE comments. Or tune the gateway.

[13:23] Hannah Schmitt: So action item: Anika, can you confirm the Cloudflare + gateway timeouts and whether it’s HTTP/2 end-to-end.

[13:31] Anika Patel: Yes.

[13:33] Simran Kaur: And please share one failing Sentry trace if possible.

[13:36] Anika Patel: Yep.

[13:38] Derek Lin: What about 429s—if we implement backoff, does that hurt end-user latency? Like if it waits.

[13:46] Simran Kaur: It can, but it’s better than immediate fail. Also you can present “retrying” in UI. Most importantly, you want to avoid retries that pile up.

[13:58] Hannah Schmitt: Also, if we bump limits and you cap concurrency, you should see fewer 429s overall.

[14:04] Derek Lin: Okay.

[14:06] Morgan Reyes: If we go production later, would this push us to Dedicated? Or can hosted handle it.

[14:12] Hannah Schmitt: Depends on your throughput and predictability needs. Many customers stay hosted with higher quotas. Dedicated is if you want guaranteed capacity and isolation and strict SLOs.

[14:23] Derek Lin: We might be in-between. We’re not huge, but we want it reliable.

[14:27] Hannah Schmitt: Totally.

[14:29] Simran Kaur: For the POC, hosted is fine. Let’s just get the client behavior stable and confirm the limits.

[14:36] Hannah Schmitt: Cool. Quick check—are you seeing any other errors besides 429 and the stream disconnect.

[14:42] Anika Patel: A couple 5xx but very low. Mostly the two.

[14:46] Simran Kaur: Okay.

[14:47] Hannah Schmitt: Do you have fallback enabled? Like switching models or regions.

[14:52] Morgan Reyes: Not yet. We talked about it but didn’t implement.

[14:56] Simran Kaur: Okay. Fallback won’t help 429s caused by your quota. But it can help if there’s a regional issue.

[15:03] Hannah Schmitt: Yep.

[15:05] Derek Lin: The only reason I ask is: if the stream dies, could you fallback mid stream.

[15:10] Simran Kaur: Not mid-stream, no. You’d need to restart the request. That’s why idempotency keys and partial outputs handling matter.

[15:21] Anika Patel: We don’t have idempotency keys right now.

[15:24] Simran Kaur: We can provide a recommended pattern: client-generated request UUID, store partial tokens, if restart, you can re-run with the same prompt but mark as retry. Not perfect, but it helps.

[15:38] Morgan Reyes: Okay.

[15:40] Hannah Schmitt: Let’s do a recap of action items so we don’t lose them.

[15:43] Hannah Schmitt: One: Anika sends timeout settings and confirmation on proxies (Cloudflare + gateway) and any Sentry traces for stream failures.

[15:52] Anika Patel: Yep.

[15:53] Hannah Schmitt: Two: Anika/Morgan send 2–3 example prompts that generate long responses and seem to trigger it.

[16:00] Morgan Reyes: Yes, we’ll redact.

[16:02] Hannah Schmitt: Three: Redwood (Simran) will look up the 429s by request_id and identify limiter type.

[16:08] Simran Kaur: Yep.

[16:09] Hannah Schmitt: Four: I’ll work with ops to bump the POC limits (burst + concurrent streams) and email you the new numbers.

[16:17] Derek Lin: Great.

[16:19] Hannah Schmitt: Five: Simran will send a suggested backoff/jitter + concurrency cap implementation for Node.

[16:25] Simran Kaur: Yep.

[16:27] Hannah Schmitt: And on the reference thing: we’ll draft a “public share boundaries” list with percent/ranges and no absolute volumes, and you’ll route to Legal.

[16:38] Derek Lin: Correct.

[16:40] Morgan Reyes: Works.

[16:41] Simran Kaur: One more: if possible, share a failing request_id for the stream disconnect. I want to check whether Redwood ended it or the client did.

[16:49] Anika Patel: I’ll try. Sometimes we don’t have request_id on stream errors.

[16:54] Simran Kaur: If you have any header capture or logs, that helps.

[16:58] Hannah Schmitt: We can also add a header echo in the SDK example so you persist it.

[17:03] Anika Patel: Yeah.

[17:05] Derek Lin: Timeline-wise, we want to run the next replay test by end of week.

[17:10] Hannah Schmitt: That’s doable. We’ll aim to have the limit bump by tomorrow and analysis by then as well.

[17:17] Morgan Reyes: And then next week we can talk about broader rollout.

[17:20] Hannah Schmitt: Perfect.

[17:22] Simran Kaur: Also, I’ll check if we can include a Retry-After header consistently on 429. If yes, you can respect it.

[17:29] Anika Patel: That would be super helpful.

[17:32] Hannah Schmitt: Great. Anything else from your side?

[17:35] Derek Lin: No, this is good. Thanks.

[17:38] Morgan Reyes: Thanks.

[17:40] Anika Patel: Thanks everyone.

[17:42] Hannah Schmitt: Cool—talk soon. Bye.

---

Auto-generated notes (Fireflies):
- Key issue: 429 spikes during burst traffic; likely concurrency limiter + aggressive retries.
- Key issue: streaming disconnect around ~60 seconds; likely gateway/idle timeout + occasional gaps in token stream.
- Next meeting: tentatively Tue/Thu next week (Hannah to send options).
